analysis.one_liner: Raises child labor penalties and lets child workers sue employers for damages.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill, introduced with one cosponsor, never received a committee hearing or a floor vote and died when Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act to make it easier to punish companies that employ children in dangerous or illegal jobs. It would extend child labor rules to minors working as independent contractors, allow children to sue their employers for compensatory and punitive damages of up to $250,000, raise maximum civil penalties to $132,270 per child (or $601,150 for repeat or willful violations) with automatic inflation increases, and add criminal penalties of up to a year in prison for repeated or willful violators. It would also fund training programs to help employers avoid violations and create an advisory committee on child labor.
analysis.who_benefits: Child workers placed in hazardous or illegal jobs, including minors working as independent contractors who today fall outside federal child labor rules. The bill would give them the right to sue for damages and give the Labor Department bigger sticks to fine violators.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children in hazardous or illegal jobs

how_it_helps.text: Extends federal child labor protections to minors working as independent contractors, closing a gap employers can use to keep children off the payroll and out of view of federal rules.
Creates a private right of action: any child harmed by a child labor violation could sue for compensatory and punitive damages of up to $250,000, in addition to Department of Labor enforcement.
Raises maximum civil penalties from $11,000 to $132,270 per violation, and from $50,000 to $601,150 for repeat or willful violations, with annual inflation adjustments so the fines keep their value.
Adds criminal penalties of up to a $50,000 fine and one year in prison for employers who repeatedly or willfully violate child labor rules.

Authorizes grants to nonprofits, employer associations, and labor organizations for education and training to prevent child labor violations, and establishes a National Advisory Committee on Child Labor.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who use child labor, and any business that employs minors and would face higher compliance costs, larger fines, and new lawsuit exposure under the private right of action.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers using underage or hazardous labor

drawbacks.text: The new private right of action with punitive damages up to $250,000 per child would expose even good-faith employers to costly litigation if they unknowingly violate the rules.
Applying child labor laws to independent contractors could sweep in legitimate teen self-employment and freelance work, since many minors earn money as contractors rather than employees.
Raising maximum civil penalties to $132,270 per violation, and $601,150 for willful violations, would substantially increase the cost of any mistake for smaller employers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real: federal child labor penalties had not kept pace with the value of the violation, and minors working as independent contractors were effectively outside the rules. The costs fall on employers, mainly through higher fines and new lawsuit exposure, and an honest supporter would acknowledge that small businesses and some legitimate teen contractor work could get caught in the net. The bill does include grants to help employers comply voluntarily, which softens the burden.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never held a hearing or voted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Brian Schatz introduced the Stop Child Labor Act on October 17, 2023, joined by Sen. Todd Young, making it a bipartisan bill.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the day it was introduced.
No further action was recorded: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who use child labor — including in agriculture, meatpacking, restaurants, and staffing or contracting arrangements — are better off because the bill died: fines stay at the old low levels, children cannot sue for damages, and minors working as independent contractors remain outside federal child labor rules.

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Stop Child Labor Act to raise child labor penalties, extend rules to independent contractors, and let child workers sue for damages.

for.name: Sen. Todd Young
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's one cosponsor, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote during the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat and a Republican, but no vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of any real contest was never tested.

industries.note: Agriculture employs far more minors than any other industry, and children working as independent contractors on farms fall outside federal child labor rules today. The bill would close that loophole and subject farm employers to much larger fines and lawsuits, so these employers had a direct financial interest in the bill going nowhere.

Cleaning companies operating inside meatpacking plants have repeatedly been found using children in hazardous overnight jobs, with federal penalties amounting to only a few thousand dollars per child in some cases. The bill's higher fines and private lawsuits would directly target this business model.

Restaurants are among the most common employers of 14- and 15-year-olds and frequently cited for hour and hazardous-duty violations. Raising the maximum civil penalty from $11,000 to $132,270 per violation would sharply raise the cost of noncompliance.

Intermediaries that supply child workers to plants and warehouses often structure minors as independent contractors to evade child labor rules. The bill would extend those rules to independent-contractor minors, ending that workaround.
